course.name: Intermediate Micro Theory
course.tagline: Consumer choice, markets and taxes, monopoly, games.

cards.simple: Complete (any two bundles can be ranked), transitive (A ≿ B and B ≿ C ⇒ A ≿ C). Usually also monotone (more is better) and convex (averages preferred to extremes).
Marginal rate of substitution: MRS = MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub>, the rate the consumer will trade y for one more x and stay indifferent. The (absolute) slope of the indifference curve.
Interior optimum: MRS = p<sub>x</sub>/p<sub>y</sub> (equivalently MU<sub>x</sub>/p<sub>x</sub> = MU<sub>y</sub>/p<sub>y</sub>) and the budget is spent: p<sub>x</sub>x + p<sub>y</sub>y = I.
U = x<sup>a</sup>y<sup>1−a</sup> ⇒ x* = aI/p<sub>x</sub>, y* = (1−a)I/p<sub>y</sub>. A constant budget share a goes to x.
In max U(x,y) s.t. p<sub>x</sub>x + p<sub>y</sub>y = I, λ* is the marginal utility of income: how much the maximized utility rises per extra dollar.
Marshallian x(p, I): maximizes utility given income. Hicksian h(p, U): minimizes the spending needed to reach utility U. Hicksian demand only has substitution effects.
∂x/∂p<sub>x</sub> = ∂h/∂p<sub>x</sub> − x·∂x/∂I. Total effect = substitution effect (always ≤ 0) + income effect.
more: See the Consumer optimizer tool for the A → B → C decomposition.

cards.simple: Normal: x rises with income. Inferior: x falls with income. Giffen: an inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so demand slopes up.
ε = (∂Q/∂P)(P/Q). |ε| > 1 elastic (raising price cuts revenue), |ε| < 1 inelastic. On linear demand, elasticity changes along the curve.
Scale all inputs by t: output rises by more than t (increasing), exactly t (constant) or less (decreasing). For K<sup>α</sup>L<sup>β</sup>, compare α + β with 1.
Marginal rate of technical substitution = MP<sub>L</sub>/MP<sub>K</sub>: the slope of the isoquant.
MP<sub>L</sub>/MP<sub>K</sub> = w/r (isoquant tangent to isocost), equivalently MP<sub>L</sub>/w = MP<sub>K</sub>/r: the last dollar buys the same output from each input.

cards.term: MC crosses AC at its minimum
cards.simple: When MC < AC, average cost falls; when MC > AC it rises. So MC cuts AC (and AVC) at their minimum points.
A competitive firm produces where P = MC as long as P ≥ min AVC. Below that it shuts down and loses only its fixed cost.
Free entry and exit drive economic profit to zero: P = MC = min AC.
CS: the area below demand and above the price paid. PS: the area above supply and below the price received.
Total surplus lost compared with the efficient outcome: trades worth more to buyers than they cost sellers that don’t happen (or inefficient trades that do).
Who bears a tax doesn’t depend on who legally pays it. The less elastic side bears more: the buyers’ share = ε<sub>S</sub>/(ε<sub>S</sub> + |ε<sub>D</sub>|).
A maximum price below equilibrium: quantity falls to what suppliers offer, causing a shortage and deadweight loss (plus search and queueing costs in practice).
No one can be made better off without making someone worse off. In an Edgeworth box these are the points where the two MRSs are equal: the contract curve.
Under perfect competition (with no externalities and full information) a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
Produce where MR = MC and charge the price on the demand curve at that quantity. With P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ.
(P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|. A monopolist always prices on the elastic part of demand (|ε| > 1).

1st degree: each buyer pays their reservation price (no DWL, no CS). 2nd: menus or quantity discounts that buyers self-select. 3rd: different prices for identifiable groups, with the higher price where demand is less elastic.
A strategy profile where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others’: no one gains by deviating alone.
A strategy that does strictly better than every alternative whatever the others do. If each player has one, that profile is the (unique) Nash equilibrium.
Each player has a dominant strategy (defect), but mutual defection is worse for both than mutual cooperation. Individual rationality ≠ collective efficiency.
Firms choose quantities simultaneously. With P = a − bQ and equal MC c: q<sub>i</sub> = (a − c)/(3b). Output lies between monopoly and competition.
Firms choose prices. With identical products and equal constant MC, the equilibrium is P = MC: two firms are enough for the competitive outcome.

questions.label: Q1
questions.prompt: U = x<sup>0.5</sup>y<sup>0.5</sup>, I = 100, p<sub>x</sub> = 2, p<sub>y</sub> = 5. Optimal x?

options.why: That’s I/p<sub>x</sub>, spending everything on x. Cobb–Douglas spends the share a = 0.5.
Used p<sub>y</sub> in place of p<sub>x</sub>: 0.5·100/5.
I/p<sub>y</sub> is the most y you can buy, not the optimal x.

questions.label: Q2
questions.prompt: The price of a normal good rises. The substitution and income effects on its quantity…

options.why: Substitution effect is always ≤ 0 for an own-price rise; real income falls and a normal good is bought less.

options.t: Substitution reduces it; income raises it
options.why: That’s the pattern for an inferior good.
Only possible in odd cases. The substitution effect never raises quantity when own price rises.

options.t: Substitution raises it; income reduces it
options.why: The substitution effect always moves away from the good that got relatively dearer.

options.t: Inferior, with an income effect larger than the substitution effect
options.why: Only then can a price rise raise quantity demanded.

options.t: Normal, with a large income effect
options.why: For a normal good both effects cut quantity when price rises.
Luxuries are normal goods (income elasticity > 1).
Inelastic demand still slopes down.

questions.label: Q4
questions.prompt: Demand P = 100 − 2Q, supply P = 10 + Q. A $6 per-unit tax is imposed. Deadweight loss?

options.why: Q falls from 30 to 28. DWL = ½·6·(30 − 28) = 6.
Forgot the ½: the DWL is a triangle.
That’s tax revenue, 6 × 28, which goes to the government rather than being lost.
A tax drives a wedge between the buyer and seller prices, so some trades don’t happen.

questions.label: Q5
questions.prompt: Same market (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 10 + Q, $6 tax). What price do buyers now pay?

options.why: Q = 28, P<sub>b</sub> = 100 − 56 = 44. Buyers bear $4 of the $6 because demand is steeper.
That assumes buyers bear the whole tax (40 + 6). Sellers bear some too.
That’s the price sellers keep: 44 − 6.
That’s the pre-tax equilibrium price.

questions.label: Q6
questions.prompt: Monopoly: demand P = 100 − 2Q, MC = 20. Profit-maximizing Q and P?

options.why: MR = 100 − 4Q = 20 ⇒ Q = 20; read P off demand: 100 − 40 = 60.
That’s the competitive outcome, P = MC.
Price comes from the demand curve, not MC.
That maximizes revenue (MR = 0) and ignores cost.

questions.label: Q7
questions.prompt: A monopolist faces |ε| = 4 at its optimum and MC = 30. Price?

options.why: Marked up MC by 1/4 (30·1.25). The Lerner index is a share of price.
Multiplied MC by |ε|.
That’s competitive pricing. A monopolist marks up when demand isn’t perfectly elastic.
CRS needs the exponents to sum to exactly 1.
Decreasing needs a sum below 1.

options.t: Diminishing returns to scale, because each exponent is below 1
options.why: Exponents below 1 mean diminishing marginal products, which is a different idea from returns to scale.

questions.label: Q9
questions.prompt: A competitive firm’s price is below minimum AVC but above zero. In the short run it should…

options.t: Shut down and lose only its fixed cost
options.why: Producing would lose fixed cost plus part of variable cost.
Only if P ≥ min AVC. Otherwise each unit adds more cost than revenue.
Firms choose output by P = MC, not by minimizing AC.
A competitive firm is a price taker.

questions.label: Q10
questions.prompt: In a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma, the Nash equilibrium is…

options.t: Both defect, even though both cooperating would make each better off
options.why: Defect is dominant for each; the equilibrium is Pareto-dominated.
Each player gains by deviating to defect, so it isn’t an equilibrium.
The cooperator would rather defect.
(Defect, Defect) is the unique (and dominant-strategy) equilibrium.

questions.label: Q11
questions.prompt: Cournot duopoly: P = 120 − Q, both firms MC = 0. Each firm produces…

options.why: 60 each gives Q = 120 and P = 0, the competitive (Bertrand) outcome.
Splitting the monopoly output (60) evenly is the collusive outcome, not Cournot.
Too low: the best response to 20 is q = (120 − 20)/2 = 50.

questions.label: Q12
questions.prompt: For U = x<sup>a</sup>y<sup>1−a</sup>, the MRS (MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub>) is…

options.why: MU<sub>x</sub> = aU/x, MU<sub>y</sub> = (1 − a)U/y.
Upside-down ratio of goods. MU<sub>x</sub> falls as x rises, so x goes in the denominator.
Missing the y/x term, so the MRS wouldn’t diminish along the curve.
That’s what MRS equals at the optimum, not its definition.
